The law in a sentence: THE LAW IN A SENTENCE California's law tells a holder to pay the owner itself if the owner proves the claim before the handover (Code of Civil Procedure 1532(b)), and lets it pay afterwards and be repaid by the State (1560(b)). 200 days to the next handover, 1 June 2027 The property is due to the State between 1 and 15 June each year (1532(a)). Once the State holds it, the only way it pays is a cheque in the post. Sources: 1532(b): general reporting information, 1560(b): holder reimbursement guide, 1532(a): how to report, Payment by cheque

Why a holder pays: WHO CAN PAY, AND WHY IT WOULD Any holder with a bank account can pay by transfer today: an employer or payroll company holding final wages, a marketplace or platform holding balances and credits, a bank, a broker, an insurer. The State cannot. It pays by a cheque in the post. It has to write to the owner anyway It may charge at most two dollars for that notice It reports twice and keeps the records for seven years If the owner answers in time, the money never goes to the State Being late costs 12 percent a year What these duties cost any one holder is not published, and no figure for it is given here. Every Airwallex call, made on the Airwallex sandbox: the corridors, rates, quotes, fees, transfers, refusals and ledger lines are what it returned. The people followed through a claim, the families of the estates, the owners in a batch and every document they show are a demonstration: invented, marked SAMPLE, and the voice is synthetic. The holder's own list is an invented file of invented owners. Notices are prepared here and never sent: the holder sends them and marks them sent. No holder uses Khutlisa yet. A holder's book is a plan made from public figures; the holder's view is this same app behind a key, and its deposit is staged on the sandbox. Documents are read, not verified with the issuing authority. The holder approves every payment. Paying an owner abroad by bank transfer under sections 1532(b) and 1560(b) is our reading of the law. The main path is the holder paying the owner directly; claiming from the State yourself is the fallback.

After it you may still pay, and the State repays you (1560(b)).
